conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a quick, well-validated questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. This isn’t a test of your parenting; it’s simply a snapshot of your emotional well-being so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve.  

Everything we discuss stays confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. There are ten short questions, each asking about the past seven days. We’ll keep the conversation natural—no need to remember any numbers or categories. Whenever you’re ready, we’ll begin.  

Question 1: In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft half-smile]  
“Most of the time I can still laugh—like when the baby makes those silly milk-drunk faces—but I notice it takes more effort. My sister told a joke yesterday that normally would’ve had me cracking up, and I only managed a little chuckle before my mind jumped back to worrying about whether the baby was breathing okay in the bassinet. So I can laugh, it just feels… muted, I guess.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah... I can still laugh, but it doesn't come as easily. Like, I *want* to find things funny, and sometimes I do, but it feels kind of forced or short-lived. I’ll smile or laugh, but then the worry creeps back in. It’s not the same light feeling I used to have.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[slow shrug]  
“Not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately it all feels like another task on the list. I still do them, hoping the good feeling will show up, but mostly I’m just going through the motions.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes... like last night when she wouldn’t settle for two hours, I kept thinking I must’ve eaten something to upset her tummy, or that I’m just not reading her cues right. I know babies cry, but my head still jumps to “this is my fault.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep in the bassinet, and suddenly my heart’s racing like something awful is about to happen. I check her breathing over and over, even when she’s fine. There’s no real reason—I just can’t shake the “what-if” loop in my head.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I have to remind myself to breathe. Nothing’s happening, the room is quiet, but my body acts like there’s danger. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales]  
“Most days I’m coping, but yeah—there are moments when the dishes, the laundry, the feeding, the constant ‘am-I-doing-this-right?’ thoughts just pile up. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly feel like I’m drowning in little chores I can’t keep up with. It’s not all the time, just… enough to make me feel stretched too thin.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not every night, but a few times this week I’ve laid down feeling wired—like my mind won’t stop replaying everything I might’ve messed up that day. Even when the baby’s asleep, I’ll lie there staring at the ceiling, and by the time I finally drift off it’s almost time for the next feed.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve had patches of that—nothing all-day-long, but I’ll be folding onesies and suddenly feel this heavy sadness settle in. It usually lifts after a bit, but while it’s there I feel kind of empty and weepy, even though I can’t always say why.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really… I’ve gotten teary a couple of times, but I haven’t actually cried—more like my eyes sting and I swallow hard and push it down. I keep telling myself I don’t have time to fall apart, so I just blink it away and keep going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
“No—never. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again, not disappear.”

You've shared that since your baby arrived laughter feels forced and fleeting, activities you once enjoyed now seem like chores, and waves of worry or even panic arrive without warning. You described moments of drowning in small tasks, blaming yourself when your daughter won't settle, and lying awake replaying the day. Yet you firmly stated you have never thought of harming yourself; you simply want to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports minimal to no anticipatory enjoyment, describing activities as joyless tasks and "going through the motions," aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, specific self-blame episodes (unsettled baby) that occur "sometimes" and meet the "some of the time" threshold.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense anxiety with physical symptoms and obsessive checking, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes occurring "a couple of times," matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm from daily tasks, indicating partial coping difficulty consistent with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple nights of racing thoughts preventing sleep, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 17 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset. You endorse core symptoms such as marked loss of enjoyment (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), frequent anxious worries and physical panic sensations, mood-linked sleep disruption, and persistent self-blame. These findings align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health specialist for full evaluation
2. Discuss evidence-based treatment options including <med>CBT</med> and/or medication compatible with breastfeeding
3. Plan daily 15-minute blocks of restorative activity (walk, shower, music) while a support person cares for the baby
4. Share your EPDS result with your obstetrician or midwife so they can coordinate follow-up
5. Use brief breathing techniques when panic sensations start: inhale 4 counts, exhale 6 counts
6. Reach out to local <med>PPD support groups</med> or the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 24/7 at 1-833-943-5746
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Screening Summary – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today’s date]  
Source: Patient self-report via EPDS-style inquiry  

**Primary areas endorsed**  
- Anhedonia/loss of pleasure (Q2) – “going through the motions,” no anticipatory enjoyment  
- Low mood with tearfulness (Q8, Q9) – episodic heavy sadness, eyes “sting,” suppresses crying  
- Sleep disturbance mood-linked (Q7) – initial insomnia ruminating about “messing up”  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame (Q3) – attributes infant crying to own actions  
- Generalized & situational anxiety: intrusive “what-ifs,” repeated checking of infant breathing (Q4)  
- Panic-style episodes: sudden chest tightness, shaking, no objective trigger (Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed / unable to cope with routine tasks (Q6) – “drowning in little chores”  

**Safety screen**  
Denies self-harm thoughts (Q10); no ideation reported.  

**Observed pattern**  
Symptoms cluster around low mood, anhedonia, prominent anxiety/panic, and functional difficulty typical of postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; intensity appears moderate, present several days per week, beginning post-delivery.  

**Screening significance**  
Total clinical picture exceeds “baby blues” threshold; meets criteria for further evaluation (probable major depressive episode with anxious features, DSM specifiers: peripartum onset). Recommend formal diagnostic interview, psychosocial support assessment, and discussion of treatment options.
